1.text: **Govern, Identify** Basis: this practice establishes baseline performance, safety, and security requirements before deployment, which falls under CSF's GOVERN (organizational context, risk strategy) and IDENTIFY (asset and process understanding, baselining) functions, consistent with the function-level pattern used at Practice 6.

**ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018**, *Systems and software engineering — Requirements engineering*. This cross-sector standard covers requirements elicitation and validation. It operates one level below the ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 process reference already cited and supports translating mission goals into verifiable, auditable requirements.

1.1.1.text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, *Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering*, which governs distilling existing documentation into a validated requirements and success-criteria summary, as this implementation describes.

1.1.2.text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (requirements traceability across stakeholders); NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1, *Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems* (cited at Practice 2), whose requirements-traceability guidance applies to mapping mission goals to a structured requirements matrix.

1.2.text: **Measure 2.5** (the AI system is evaluated for validity and reliability against defined baselines); **Measure 2.6** (the AI system is evaluated for safety risk under normal and stressed conditions).
**Identify** (establishing quantitative baselines is asset and process characterization).

NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1 (baseline and impact characterization, used at Practice 2); ANSI/ISA-62443-3-3-2013 §11 Resource Availability (cited at Practice 2), relevant to baselining performance under stress.

1.2.1.text: "Document the current (pre-AI) performance and safety envelope of the manual or legacy process using existing operational records, historical incident logs, and subject-matter-expert interviews, capturing both steady-state performance and known failure modes. This baseline is the comparison point required by Task 1.2 and should be re-validated whenever the underlying process changes materially."
NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1; NIST SP 800-82r3 (cited at Practice 2 for OT baseline and impact characterization).

1.2.2.text: "Extend the baseline from Implementation 1.2.1 with quantitative performance data captured under abnormal, degraded, or high-load conditions (for example, peak demand, component failure, adverse weather), drawn from historical incident data, simulation, or controlled stress testing where it is safe to do so. This is the baseline against which Task 2.3's TEVV protocols and Implementation 2.3.4's recurrent risk evaluations later measure performance drift."

1.3.2.text: DoD Manual 5000.101 (cited at Task 1.3), whose process for tiering OT&E/LFT&E environments for AI-enabled systems applies here; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 (Software testing) for general test-environment fidelity and categorization vocabulary.

1.3.3.text: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (AI 100-1), MEASURE function (the anchor reference for Task 1.3); ISO/IEC 25010 (Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — SQuaRE) for structured behavior-against-requirements evaluation criteria.

1.3.4.text: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5, AU (Audit and Accountability) control family; ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A.6 (used elsewhere in the reviewer community's crosswalk work for evidence and documentation control).

1.4.1.text: sector-specific terminology and data-dictionary standards are the right anchor here rather than a single cross-sector reference, for example ISO 15926 (industrial automation data integration for operations and maintenance) for process industries, or the equivalent sector data dictionary (IEC 61850 common information model for power systems; HL7/SNOMED CT for healthcare). Recommend flagging this sub-field for sector-specific companion guidance rather than a single cross-sector citation.

1.4.2.text: same treatment as TBD-013. This is likely better served by a sector-specific companion reference (for example, plain-language or accessibility standards for administrative-facing AI outputs) than a single cross-sector citation. Flag as sector-specific.

1.4.4.text: NIST SP 800-218A (the anchor reference for this Practice); OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications (cited at Task 5.3) for AI-generated-code and configuration risk vocabulary.

2.text: **Measure 2.5** (validity and reliability), **Measure 2.6** (safety), **Measure 2.7** (security and resilience); **Map 2.3** (TEVV and scientific integrity); **Manage 2.2** (resilience to negative impacts). This matches the mapping already established in this project's Practices-Index reference table.
**Protect, Detect** (maintaining QoS under degraded conditions is a protective-control function; detecting deviation from baseline is a detection function).

2.field: References* (the trailing TBD attached to the DHS-CISA Zero Trust for OT citation)
2.text: Three of the four listed references already have explanatory text; only the DHS-CISA "Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology" entry is missing its blurb. Suggested annotation: "Applies zero-trust segmentation and continuous-verification principles to OT environments, providing a model for containing AI-driven performance degradation from spreading across control-system boundaries."

**NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1**, *Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems*. This is the companion volume to the Vol. 1 reference already cited and focuses on resilience techniques rather than general systems engineering, which fits this practice's "Resilient" trustworthiness characteristic.

3.text: Agentic behavior; Guardrails; Human-in-the-loop / human-on-the-loop; Risk tolerance; Deterministic boundaries. Note: this practice's *Primary Cyber AI Profile Mappings* field carries its own TBD. The reviewer note from Boone Carlson referenced in the discussion-thread file points to OWASP LLM06 "Complete Mediation," the Five Eyes Agentic AI Joint Guidance, and CISA's OT AI-integration principles as candidates for that field, worth pulling into the mapping once it is populated.

**OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications (2025)**. It is cited at Task 5.3 for identity and privilege abuse. At the practice level it anchors the broader agentic-risk taxonomy this practice governs, not only the access-control portion.

4.text: Human-in-the-loop; Break-glass override; Situational awareness; Fail-safe; Human-on-the-loop / human-out-of-the-loop.
**Respond, Recover** (this practice concerns emergency intervention and restoring safe operation, the CSF Respond and Recover functions).

**DHS-CISA *Principles for the Secure Integration of AI in Operational Technology*, §4.2 (Embed Safety and Failsafe Mechanisms)**. Section 4.2 of a document already cited at Practice 1 addresses override and recovery procedures, so a cross-reference at this practice level is warranted.

5.text: **Identify, Protect** (asset and identity inventory, plus access-control enforcement).

**NIST SP 800-63-4**, *Digital Identity Guidelines*. This is a foundational identity-assurance standard rather than an AI- or cyber-specific one, and it is not superseded by the Cyber AI Profile's guidance. It gives the practice a vocabulary (identity assurance levels, authenticator assurance levels) that applies whether or not the AI entity is treated as a cybersecurity concern, which answers the reviewer's request for a non-duplicative angle.

5.1.text: **Govern 1.6** (AI system inventory); **Map 1.1** (operating context, since this task defines what counts as a distinct "AI entity" needing an identity).

5.1.2.text: "Issue a distinct machine identity (service account, workload identity, or equivalent non-human identity) to each AI agent or tool invocation at the granularity determined in Task 5.1, rather than reusing a single shared credential across multiple agents or falling back to a human operator's identity. Every credential should be traceable to exactly one accountable owner responsible for provisioning, rotation, and revocation of that identity."

5.1.3.text: "Require that AI entities authenticate to systems, tools, and each other using cryptographically verifiable credentials (for example, short-lived signed tokens, mutual TLS, or an equivalent workload-identity mechanism) rather than static shared secrets. Authentication should be automated and enforced at the point of action so that no AI entity can act on protected systems without presenting a valid, verifiable credential."

5.2.text: **Govern 1.6** (inventory and resourcing per risk priority); **Manage 3.1** (monitoring third-party and component risk, where access spans external tools).

5.2.1.text: "Produce and maintain a documented mapping from each AI entity (per Task 5.1) to the specific systems, data sources, and tools it is authorized to access, including the operational justification for that access. This mapping is the authoritative source for the technical enforcement and audit required by Task 5.2, and should be reviewed on a defined cadence and whenever the AI entity's function changes."

5.2.2.text: "Where static role-based access is insufficient, implement access-control policies that evaluate current operational context (for example, time of day, system state, or task in progress) before granting an AI entity access to a resource, rather than granting standing access for the lifetime of the credential. This limits the blast radius of a compromised or misbehaving AI entity to what is contextually appropriate at the moment of the request."

5.2.3.text: "Determine, using the factors identified in Task 5.1 (available resources, threat level, impact, scale, application complexity), the practical granularity at which agent identities, protected assets, and permissions should be defined and reviewed. Document the rationale so that granularity decisions can be revisited as those factors change, consistent with the flexible approach called for in Task 5.1."

5.3.text: **Govern 1.6** (inventory and resourcing by risk); **Manage 2.1** (managing AI risks in proportion to potential impact), since least-privilege and least-agency enforcement is a direct control on residual risk.
**NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-6** (Least Privilege). This is the sector-agnostic access-control anchor beneath the agentic-specific OWASP reference already cited.

5.3.1.text: "For each AI entity and task pairing, determine the minimum set of permissions and tool-invocation capabilities required to complete that task, starting from zero access and adding only what is demonstrably necessary, rather than starting from a broad template and attempting to subtract. Apply this minimum-permission set as the default, with any broader access requiring documented, time-bound justification."

5.3.2.text: "Enforce least-agency limits automatically rather than relying on policy alone: bound each AI entity's session to a defined set of permitted actions and a maximum duration or action count, after which the session must be re-authorized. This prevents an AI entity from silently accumulating standing capability beyond what Implementation 5.3.1 authorized for that specific task."

5.4.text: **NIST SP 800-137**, *Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations*. It provides the continuous-monitoring process framework that complements the MITRE ATLAS attack-pattern taxonomy already cited.

5.4.1.text: "Log every authentication event, access grant, and access denial associated with an AI entity's identity, including the identity, target resource, and outcome, and review these logs on a defined cadence for irregular patterns. This log stream feeds both the audit capabilities required by Practice 10 and the anomaly-detection monitoring in Implementation 5.4.2."

5.4.2.text: "Extend existing SOC monitoring to include AI-entity-specific behavioral baselines (for example, typical access patterns, request volume, and resource scope per entity) and alert on deviations in real time, rather than relying solely on periodic log review. Where feasible, correlate these alerts with the anomaly monitoring described in Task 3.4 to distinguish access-layer anomalies from broader behavioral drift."

6.2.1.text: "Require that every externally sourced AI component (model, API, dataset, or agentic-platform dependency) be registered in the organization's existing asset management system before production use, recording the vendor, version, intended use, and the accountable internal owner for that component. This extends standard IT/OT asset management practice to AI components rather than creating a parallel, disconnected inventory."

6.2.2.text: "Route vendor-initiated model or component updates through the organization's existing change-management process rather than allowing silent, unmanaged updates, and use runtime telemetry to detect behavioral shifts that suggest an update occurred without notification. This applies standard IT change control to a class of dependency (externally hosted models) that can change behavior without a corresponding code change on the organization's side."

6.2.3.text: "Define and execute a decommissioning process for externally sourced AI components reaching vendor end-of-life or contract termination, including migration or fallback planning, before the vendor's support obligation ends. This mirrors the internal decommissioning process defined in Task 7.6 but addresses the added complexity of vendor-controlled timelines and data-return or deletion obligations."

6.3.1.text: "Identify and document every point at which data leaves the organization's environment to an external AI vendor or platform (for example, inference requests, telemetry, fine-tuning data), along with the specific third-party destination and processing purpose for each. This catalog is the prerequisite for the egress monitoring and data-handling controls required elsewhere in Task 6.3."

6.3.2.text: "Monitor data egress against the catalog built in Implementation 6.3.1 and flag transfers to undocumented destinations or in unexpected volume. Where sensitive operational data must be used for external training or telemetry, route it through an isolated, access-restricted enclave that limits what leaves the enclave to the minimum necessary for the vendor relationship."

7.text: Data provenance; Shadow AI; Version control; Configuration management; Fine-tuning.

**Map 4.1** (mapping AI technology and legal risks of components, the internal counterpart to the same category used at Practice 6); **Manage 1.4** (negative residual risk from internal supply-chain gaps); **Govern 1.6** (inventory).
**Identify, Protect** (mirrors Practice 6's mapping, since Practice 7 is the internal counterpart to Practice 6's external supply-chain visibility).

NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 (Cyber Supply Chain Risk Management, C-SCRM), established elsewhere in this reviewer community's reference index as the anchor for internal and organizational supply-chain risk management; ISO/IEC 5962:2021 (SPDX) for the AI and software bill-of-materials mechanics that Task 6.1 references at the external-vendor level and that apply to internally tracked components.

8.text: Root cause analysis; Digital chain of custody; Incident response; Forensics; Disclosure.

**Measure 3.1–3.3** (mechanisms for tracking, responding to, and communicating AI risks and incidents, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Manage 4.1** (post-deployment monitoring), **Manage 4.3** (incidents communicated to relevant AI actors).
**Respond, Recover** (incident analysis and response is the direct CSF analog).

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations, cited at Practice 4) as the general incident-handling anchor, extended here for AI-aware forensics; MITRE ATLAS (cited at Task 5.4) for AI-specific attack and failure taxonomy useful in root-cause classification.

8.4.1.text: "Add AI-specific trigger conditions (for example, confirmed AI-driven safety event, unauthorized AI action, or AI system compromise) to the organization's existing incident disclosure and regulatory reporting protocols, rather than building a parallel AI-only reporting pathway. This ensures AI incidents are routed through the same accountable disclosure process as any other operational incident, with sector-specific regulators added where the existing protocol does not already cover them."

8.4.2.text: "Where sector regulation requires notification within a fixed window (for example, financial-services suspicious-activity reporting deadlines, or sector-specific outage reporting), automate the trigger-to-notification pathway for confirmed AI-driven incidents so that the disclosure deadline is met without depending on manual escalation, and ensure the automated notice includes the impact detail the specific regulator requires."

8.5.1.text: "Pre-identify (even without a signed retainer) at least one external AI forensic specialist and one legal counsel with relevant AI incident experience, and document their contact path for activation during an incident. Where dedicated AI forensic vendors are not available or affordable, identify sector ISAC or Sector Coordinating Council mutual-aid contacts, or academic partners, as an interim substitute, consistent with the interim approaches noted in Task 8.5's description."

8.5.2.text: "Where budget allows, convert the contingency contacts identified in Implementation 8.5.1 into a formal retainer or standing services agreement, so that response time during an actual incident is not gated on new-vendor procurement. Review the retainer roster annually as the market for AI forensic services matures, per the 'currently nascent' caveat noted in this task's description."

9.text: Automation bias; Competency mapping; Workforce readiness; Calibrated trust.

**Govern 2.2** (AI risk management training for personnel and partners, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Govern 4.1** (organizational practices to cultivate a critical-thinking, safety-first culture).
**Govern** (workforce training and role-based competency is a governance-function control in CSF terms and does not map cleanly to a technical Protect or Detect function).

NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 and NIST SP 800-181 (NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity) as the established model for role-based competency mapping, extended here to AI risk roles; the automation-bias literature cited in the parallel discussion-thread work (Parasuraman & Manzey, *Complacency and bias in human use of automation*, Human Factors 52(3), 2010) is a candidate for Task 9.2 specifically.

9.1.1.text: "For each existing operational role (not a new AI-specific job title), determine the minimum AI literacy and risk-awareness level needed to safely perform that role's current responsibilities, ranging from basic awareness for occasional AI-output consumers to deep technical competency for those configuring or overriding AI systems. Use this to right-size training investment rather than applying uniform training across all roles."

9.1.2.text: "Consolidate the per-role requirements from Implementation 9.1.1 into a single competency matrix mapping roles to required competencies and current gaps, and use it to assign individualized training paths rather than a one-size-fits-all curriculum. Revisit the matrix whenever a role's exposure to AI systems changes materially."

9.3.1.text: "Record completion of required AI risk training and any associated proficiency assessment scores per individual, tied to the role-based requirements from Task 9.1, in a form that can be produced on demand for regulatory or internal audit review. This is the minimum audit-ready evidence layer beneath the readiness drills in Implementation 9.3.2."

9.3.2.text: "For roles identified as critical under Implementation 9.1.1 (for example, those authorized to override AI systems under Practice 4), require periodic hands-on readiness drills or simulations in addition to training completion, with a validated certification renewal cadence. This closes the gap between completed training and demonstrated capability under pressure."

10.text: Telemetry; Audit trail; Traceability; Chain of custody; Tamper-evidence.

**Measure 2.8** (transparency and accountability, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Govern 1.4–1.5** (documentation and reporting mechanisms); **Manage 4.1** (post-deployment monitoring).
**Detect, Identify** (logging and audit is the evidentiary backbone for detection and for maintaining an accurate operational picture).

**NIST SP 800-92 Rev. 1**, *Guide to Computer Security Log Management*, the cross-sector logging standard beneath the more recent OMB memo already cited. **ISO/IEC 27037:2012** (identification, collection, and preservation of digital evidence) is also worth adding for the tamper-evidence and chain-of-custody requirements referenced later in Task 10.2.

10.3.1.text: "Establish a defined cadence (for example, weekly or monthly, scaled to system criticality) for a qualified reviewer to manually examine AI system logs for signs of performance degradation, drift, or emerging bias not already caught by automated monitoring. Document findings and route any confirmed issues into the anomaly-handling process defined under Task 3.4."

10.3.2.text: "Build automated trend analysis and dashboards over the log data captured under Task 10.1 so that drift and anomaly signals are visible continuously rather than only at the manual-review cadence set in Implementation 10.3.1. Automated dashboards should flag threshold breaches for the manual reviewer rather than replace human judgment on borderline cases."

11.text: Business continuity; Disaster recovery; Graceful degradation; Fail-to-manual; Restoration priority.

**Manage 2.4** (mechanisms in place to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate unreliable behavior, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Manage 4.1, 4.3** (monitoring and incident communication); **Govern 1.7** (processes for decommissioning or disengaging AI systems safely).

**Recover** (this practice's core subject, restoring essential functions after an AI-driven disruption, is the direct CSF Recover function; Respond may also apply where continuity planning overlaps with active incident handling).

NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 (Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems) as the general continuity-planning anchor; ISO 22301:2019 (Business Continuity Management Systems) as the cross-sector standard already flagged as relevant to this practice elsewhere in this reviewer community's crosswalk work; NIST SP 800-82r3 §6.2.4.5 (cited at Task 11.2) for OT-specific graceful-degradation guidance.

11.1.1.text: "Rank the organization's operational processes by the severity of impact if their supporting AI component became unavailable or failed, using the same impact criteria the organization already applies to non-AI business-continuity planning where possible, rather than building a separate AI-specific criticality scale. This ranking drives the resource pre-allocation decisions in Task 11.3."

11.1.2.text: "Extend the ranking in Implementation 11.1.1 into a full dependency map showing which sector-critical functions rely, directly or indirectly, on which AI components, including cases where an AI dependency is embedded several layers deep in a vendor's own stack. This map is what prevents hidden AI dependencies from being missed during continuity planning."

11.2.1.text: "For each AI-dependent control point identified in Implementation 11.1.1 and 11.1.2, document the minimum manual procedure needed to keep the function operating, even at reduced efficiency, without the AI component. This is the entry-level continuity artifact that Implementation 11.2.2's validated Safe Operating Mode builds on for the highest-criticality functions."

11.2.2.text: "For the highest-criticality functions identified in Task 11.1, develop and formally validate a Safe Operating Mode: a complete, tested operating procedure that runs entirely independently of AI infrastructure, rather than relying on the informal fallback documented in Implementation 11.2.1. Validation should include the periodic drills required under Task 11.5."

11.3.1.text: "Identify and document the specific personnel (by role, with backup coverage) and physical tools or equipment required to execute the manual fallback and Safe Operating Mode procedures from Task 11.2, and confirm their availability on the same cadence as other continuity resources. This is distinct from Task 8.5's forensic and investigative resourcing: this task secures the resources to keep the function running, not to investigate why it failed."

11.3.2.text: "Maintain standby infrastructure (for example, non-AI backup control systems, isolated network segments, or reserve capacity) in a state ready for activation, and periodically verify, not just assume, that it remains functional and isolated from the primary AI-dependent infrastructure it is meant to replace."

11.4.1.text: "Define a mandatory pre-re-engagement checklist, referencing the TEVV protocols established in Task 1.3, that must be completed and signed off before an AI system is returned to active control after an outage or manual-mode period. The checklist should verify both technical health and that no undetected configuration drift occurred while the system was offline."

11.4.2.text: "Before fully returning control to the AI system, run it in shadow mode, receiving live inputs and producing recommendations without executing them, alongside the active manual or fallback control, and compare outputs for a defined validation period. Require mandatory safety-interlock checks to pass before shadow mode is allowed to transition to active control."

11.5.1.text: "Conduct at least annual tabletop exercises walking key personnel through a simulated AI failure and the transition to manual fallback procedures from Task 11.2, without requiring actual system disruption. Use findings to update the manual procedures and the personnel and resource pre-allocation from Task 11.3."

11.5.2.text: "For the highest-criticality functions, supplement tabletop exercises with high-fidelity simulation drills that exercise a full AI infrastructure loss and the complete recovery sequence through Task 11.4's re-commissioning checklist, at a cadence proportionate to the function's criticality tier. These drills provide the strongest evidence of organizational preparedness and should surface gaps tabletop exercises alone would miss."

12.text: Plausible hallucination; Formal specification; Code review; Machine-authored artifacts; Rollback.

**Measure 2.1** (test sets), **Measure 2.3** (performance), **Measure 2.5** (validity and reliability), **Measure 2.9** (explainability); **Map 3.1** (AI capabilities and limitations relative to context); **Manage 1.1** (achievement of intended purpose). This matches the mapping already established in this project's Practices-Index reference table.
**Protect** (validation and verification of machine-authored artifacts before they can act on infrastructure is a preventive control, closest to CSF Protect).

NIST AI 600-1 (cited at Task 12.2) as the general anchor; ANSI/CTA-2135 or ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A.6 (both identified as candidate crosswalks for this practice in this project's reference-index work) for formal validation-process standards applicable to AI-generated code and configuration review.

1.1.text: **NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1**, *Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems*. It is already cited at Practice 2 for baseline and impact characterization, and its requirements-traceability guidance applies to cataloging the functional, safety, and performance requirements this task calls for.

1.3.text: **ISO/IEC TS 4213:2022**, *Assessment of machine learning classification performance*. This is a concrete evaluation standard that complements the process-level DoD references with a specific measurement methodology, and it applies well beyond classification-heavy sectors.

1.3.1.text: **ANSI/ISA-84.00.01-2004 (IEC 61511)**, *Functional Safety: Safety Instrumented Systems for the Process Industry Sector*. It is cited at Task 4.5 for its safety-integrity-level concept, which provides a cross-sector precedent for scaling TEVV rigor to the consequence severity that this implementation's risk assessment identifies.

2.4.3.text: **NIST AI 600-1**, *Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile*. It is cited at Task 12.2 for validating AI-authored logic against "plausible hallucination" risk, and the same guidance applies to the diagnostic and maintenance-summary accuracy audits described here.

2.5.1.text: **NIST AI 100-2e2025**, *Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations*. It is cited at Task 7.2 for data-integrity concerns, and its treatment of distribution shift and out-of-specification behavior is relevant to training systems that must generalize safely beyond their observed operating range.

3.1.1.text: **IEC 60812:2018**, *Failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA and FMECA)*. This is an established cross-sector method for identifying decision points and the potential outcomes of failure at each one, which matches what this implementation asks organizations to document.

3.2.2.text: **IEC 61511** (Safety Instrumented Systems), cited at Task 4.5. Its treatment of a safe operating envelope and boundary logic independent of the primary control system fits this implementation's deterministic-constraint concept.

3.2.3.text: **IEC 61508-1**, *Functional safety of electrical/electronic/programmable electronic safety-related systems — General requirements*. It is cited at Practice 4 for general functional-safety principles, and Part 1 specifically addresses fail-safe state definition.

3.3.text: - New candidate: **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, IR-6** (Incident Reporting), for the organizational notification-protocol layer above the alarm-management guidance already cited. - Completing "ANSI/ISA-62443-3-3 (TBD)": **SR 2.8** (Auditable events) and **SR 6.1** (Audit log accessibility) are the sections relevant to notification requirements. - Completing "NIST SP 800-82r3 (TBD)": **§6.2.1** (anomaly detection and alerting guidance) is the section relevant to this task.

3.3.2.text: **NIST AI 100-2e2025** (as at CAND-007, its drift and distribution-shift taxonomy applies here) with **ISO 7870 series** (Control charts) for the statistical-process-control methodology used to set quantitative drift thresholds. Both are established cross-sector techniques.

3.7.text: **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-8 / CM-10 / CM-11** (Component Inventory / Software Usage Restrictions / User-Installed Software). This is the standard configuration-management control family for governing unauthorized or unvetted software entering an environment, which applies to the "Shadow AI" problem this task addresses.

4.4.text: **ISO 11064** (Ergonomic design of control centres). It covers control-room and operator-attention ergonomics across control-room-based CI sectors such as power, water, and transportation, complementing the alarm-specific standards already listed.

4.5.text: **IEC 61508-3** (Software requirements for safety-related systems). This is the software-specific companion to the systems-level IEC 61511 reference already cited and applies to specifying the deterministic automated protections this task requires.

5.1.1.text: **NIST SP 800-63B** (Authentication and Lifecycle Management), the credential-lifecycle companion to the SP 800-63-4 suite above, which applies to issuing and rotating machine credentials for AI entities.

6.1.4.text: **NIST SP 800-218**, *Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)*. This is the framework the discussion draft's own organizing structure was inspired by, per the project's first discussion question. Citing it here, alongside the joint **CISA "Secure by Design"** guidance, grounds this implementation's "Resilient-by-Design" concept in the SSDF's existing "Secure-by-Design" language that the implementation body text already references.

7.2.text: **ISO/IEC 5259 series**, *Data quality for analytics and machine learning*. This is a cross-sector standard for documenting internal dataset quality, source, and provenance, complementing the adversarial and poisoning focus of the NIST AI 100-2e2025 reference with a data-quality focus.

7.3.3.text: **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3** (Configuration Change Control). It fits treating "freezing model weights" as a formal change-control gate, consistent with the version-control framing that Task 7.3 already uses.

7.5.3.text: **ISO/IEC 29134:2023**, *Guidelines for privacy impact assessment*, a cross-sector standard for structuring the PIA process this implementation calls for, with the **NIST Privacy Framework 1.0** also worth citing here as NIST's companion framework to the AI RMF.

8.1.2.text: **ISO/IEC 27043:2015**, *Incident investigation principles and processes*. It establishes the baseline digital-forensics assumptions (reproducibility, evidence integrity) against which this implementation's point can be framed: that certain AI system classes structurally cannot satisfy those assumptions.

8.1.5.text: **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions**, a vendor-neutral technical standard for agent and LLM observability that addresses telemetry spanning agent-to-agent boundaries, which is the multi-agent traceability gap this implementation targets. This is an actively evolving standard rather than a mature one, but currently one of the few concrete technical references in the space.

9.2.1.text: **NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1**, *Building a Cybersecurity and Privacy Awareness and Training Program*. It provides a structural template for the role-specific curriculum this implementation calls for, complementing the automation-bias literature (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) already suggested for this practice's References field in the companion TBD-Suggestions document.

11.2.text: **NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1**, *Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems*, the general continuity-planning anchor already suggested at the Practice 11 level in the companion TBD-Suggestions document and reinforced here at the task level. **ISO 22301:2019** (Business Continuity Management Systems) is a cross-sector structural template for the "Manual Mode" playbooks this task calls for.

12.2.text: **IEEE 7001-2021**, *Transparency of Autonomous Systems*, which provides criteria for validating machine-authored logic against explainability and tacit-knowledge scrutiny, complementing NIST AI 600-1's safety and accuracy focus with a transparency lens. **ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A.6** (flagged elsewhere in this project's reference-index work as a candidate crosswalk for this practice) also fits the management-system-level validation controls this task describes.
